title: Design Direction For Legacy To Modern Transitions
excerpt: Design direction for legacy-to-modern transitions defines how an existing product can be changed without discarding the operational knowledge embedded in its interface. bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Design direction for legacy-to-modern transitions applies when an existing product has accumulated interface structures, control philosophies, vocabulary, workflow assumptions, or product concepts over many years. The work is not a visual refresh. It is a disciplined distinction between essential complexity that must remain and accidental complexity that can be removed.

The central question is what must remain. Existing interface patterns often encode institutional knowledge about a domain, a user base, or an installed operational environment. Creative Navy's legacy-to-modern transition work reads that knowledge before changing the product, then defines a migration path that existing users can realistically follow.

## When legacy-to-modern design direction is needed

Legacy-to-modern design direction is needed when accumulated complexity prevents a product from remaining usable, adoptable, or extendable, while full replacement would discard important operational knowledge. The condition can appear in mature expert software, enterprise SaaS, industrial control HMI, embedded controllers, or portfolio-level systems.

In Gexcon CFD simulation, the starting condition was a 15-year product with accumulated interface complexity and no architectural framework. The client brief was explicit: extend the product's life by 25 years. That made the engagement a platform life extension brief rather than a conventional redesign brief.

In IDEXX Animana, an 11-year platform had grown through acquisition and years of feature addition. Creative Navy provided an independent evidence-based assessment and a 5-year product vision. The engagement was assessment and direction, not full execution.

In Gericke industrial HMI, the ageing Easydos Pro interface and the separate STP61 conveying control had accreted different operating philosophies across separately commissioned product work. The condition included confused menu structure, parameter naming that had been extended without considering usability, and raw error codes. This is the legacy condition described in Creative Navy's documentation as sense decay and fragmented control philosophies.

In AIT, the legacy constraint was social rather than technical. Thousands of installers were trained on the existing controller structure, so the cost of change was expected to appear as support-call volume if installers could no longer find settings.

## What Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method preserves and changes

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

In legacy-to-modern transitions, Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats the existing product as evidence. Legacy workflows, naming conventions, interface structures, and operator habits are not discarded by default. They are examined to determine whether they represent genuine operational knowledge or only accumulated convention.

The working distinction is essential complexity versus accidental complexity. Essential complexity is load-bearing: scientific parameters, proven algorithms, regulatory or operational logic, installed competence, and workflows that expert users depend on. Accidental complexity is accumulated without purpose: inconsistent naming, duplicated interaction models, menu structures that grew without a structural framework, vocabulary that exposes the builder's data model, and product architecture that no longer matches the user's operational reality.

This is a constraint respecting form of design direction. The aim is not to make a complex product appear simple by removing capability. The aim is to make necessary complexity navigable while eliminating interface overhead that no longer serves the product or its users.

## Evidence from platform life extension and expert-software transitions

Gexcon CFD simulation is the most complete platform life extension example in this capability. Creative Navy documented 102 tasks to distinguish essential scientific and simulation complexity from accidental interface structures accumulated over 15 years of development. The design work was preceded by domain learning through calibration manuals, training videos, workplace observations, and intensive stakeholder sessions. Franz Zdravistch, Chief Training Engineer, said: "I can't believe how much you learned on your own in three days, even some of the experts I train need more time."

The Gexcon transition preserved scientific rigour while reducing interface overhead. In real deployments, time to first successful simulation changed from 4 days to 6 hours, and configuration errors changed from 5–8 to 1–2. Active users per team changed from 1 to 3–4 on a client-reported basis. Training changed from 3-day instructor-led events to webinars as an operational change. The engagement included 7 months of execution and a 2-year Implementation Partnership, where the transition was tested against development and preserved.

IDEXX Animana demonstrates the assessment and planning stage of the same capability. Research covered 35 clinics, 150+ participants, 2 weeks, and 3 countries, with 4 role types ranging from first-week users to ten-year veterans. The research separated learning-curve friction from structural problems embedded in the platform. The central finding was that 11 years of feature additions had produced an interface that no longer reflected the operational reality of veterinary practice. The most structurally significant conclusion was that reception and clinical roles had incompatible cognitive requirements requiring distinct interfaces. Creative Navy delivered 100+ recommendations structured for direct development ticket translation and a 5-year product vision.

Polymatica shows a vocabulary and structural metaphor transition. The platform was built around OLAP-specific concepts such as the cube metaphor, dimensions and facts terminology, and database-level connection flows. The transformation preserved full analytical capability while changing how users accessed it: "cube" became "dataset", "facts" became "measures", and the database connection flow was replaced with a data preparation and preview step. The lobby concept provided a central orientation point where users could see datasets described in accessible terms before entering operations. Product analytics recorded independent task completion changing from 2% to 56%.

Chemical Watch shows a product model transition rather than only an interface transition. The product changed from a news and information publication into a compliance intelligence platform. Creative Navy's design work introduced feature concepts such as the My Substances register, a regulatory intelligence workspace, and a lens-view as a persistent research environment. The subscription price tripled following platform launch on a client-reported basis. A 24x EBITDA exit multiple was reported one year after launch; the supported causal chain is design, user adoption of new features, justified price increase, revenue, and valuation. The design did not cause the exit. The design contributed to the product's ability to command a higher price.

## Evidence from embedded and industrial control transitions

Gericke industrial HMI is the clearest embedded industrial example of preserving essential complexity while changing the interaction layer. The essential part was immovable: the dosing algorithm was proven over years, and stakeholders independently insisted that it must not change. Creative Navy redesigned the interaction layer around that fixed engine, preserving essential complexity while eliminating fragmented control philosophies, confused menus, and raw error codes.

Continuity for existing Gericke users was unusually strong. The brief was explicitly not to reinvent the visual language, but to improve usability, clarity, and workflow within a recognisable Gericke environment. The legacy interface was treated as institutional knowledge because experienced operators could run it through memorised competence. Hard hardware constraints also bounded the transition: a 1024×600 panel floor and the Beckhoff/TwinCAT ecosystem were fixed parameters.

Gericke also provides the clearest design system evidence in this capability. Creative Navy created an 89-component design system as a reusable foundation for Gericke's future digital products. Gericke's own team subsequently propagated it across other product lines without Creative Navy. This is evidence for design system as evolvable architecture: the design system was not only a delivery artefact for one interface, but a structure that Gericke could extend without recreating the accumulated complexity it replaced.

Gericke client-measured outcomes were recorded within a confirmed single-variable window. There were no hardware, sensor, mechanical, training, recipe, or process changes; the window was four months post-go-live, and three sites were described by type and geography. Fault-diagnosis time was roughly two-thirds faster, with examples of 24 → 8, 38 → 12, and 68 → 20 minutes. Repeat alarms were more than halved, with examples of 42% → 18%, 58% → 28%, and 73% → 35%. Operator-caused stoppages were roughly halved, and MTTR was substantially reduced. These are framed as interface-attributable within the confirmed window, not as caused by the interface alone.

AIT is a second embedded legacy transition, but the legacy was social rather than technical. A monochrome, knob-driven controller with a deeply nested settings tree was replaced by a colour widget interface that still had to remain operable by the same rotary knob: roughly 90 steps per revolution, turn to move, press to confirm. Touch was optional throughout; if the touchscreen were dropped from the specification, the whole concept still had to work on the knob.

The AIT transition preserved recognisability where the installed base depended on it. The settings structure remained close to the one installers already knew, while orientation was added through a breadcrumb trail and a unique numeric identifier on every menu item so support staff could direct an installer to a setting by number over the telephone. Access switching was also promoted to an explicit role-selection step before PIN entry, rather than remaining buried in a settings tree as in the previous generation. No performance, efficiency, commissioning-time, error-rate, commercial, or user-tested outcome is established for AIT in this capability evidence.

## Evidence from inherited, client-diagnosed, and phased portfolio transitions

Assemblio is a variant where the client had already diagnosed the mechanism of accumulated drift. The client could describe that features were built at different points in time but could not get out from inside the resulting product structure. The examples were the client's own account while demonstrating the product: three different renaming interactions for three entity types, drag and drop not being possible for moving a project into a folder, a folder being undeletable until everything inside it had been deleted individually, export being buried in a sub-menu, annotation tools not being standardised, no undo, and copy camera / paste camera working one step at a time. These are not Creative Navy audit findings.

Oceaneering is an example of a reasoned predecessor that still required second-generation redesign. The predecessor specification already contained rational decisions, including a station-numbering convention tied to floor labels, an 11×5 area-representation grid, a 70×70-pixel thumb-target size at 1024 pixels, and per-area destination menus that pre-selected likely options and filtered out invalid ones. The semi-automatic dispatch idea already existed. The case is not the rescue of careless work; it shows how a reasoned design accumulated incoherence across a decade and two installations.

Some Oceaneering conventions were inherited and systematised rather than invented. The flashing and steady convention partly existed already at one site for sends only. The redesign generalised it across sends and receives, gave it a stated rule, and added non-colour channels. Letterforms survived icon alternatives because the installed base read them from across the room. Directional icons were added as a secondary channel.

The maritime traffic software portfolio shows phased introduction as a brief-level constraint. The client is a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators. Existing deployments would not all be replaced at once, functionality could not be removed without technical and customer approval, and the design had to permit gradual introduction across applications and future versions.

The design answer in the maritime traffic software portfolio was a four-layer token architecture: raw colours, spacing, and type scale; semantic tokens naming meaning rather than appearance; component contracts with anatomy and valid states; and bounded product compositions. The layering allowed a product to adopt semantic meaning before adopting composition. The recommended release sequence ordered adoption by risk rather than by product importance: the reference product first in one controlled configuration, then the geospatially similar products, and communications last after hardware and transmission-state verification.

## What this capability produces

Creative Navy's legacy-to-modern transition work produces a migration path, not only an endpoint design. The migration path is designed for the people and teams that must move from the existing system to the new one: expert users with memorised workflows, installers trained on a previous structure, operators reading state from across a room, development teams that must extend the design system, or product teams that must implement recommendations over several years.

The outputs vary by engagement. In Gexcon, the output included a redesign direction supported by 102 documented tasks and a 2-year Implementation Partnership. In IDEXX Animana, the output was an evidence-based assessment, 100+ recommendations, and a 5-year product vision. In Gericke, the output included an 89-component design system and 12-month Implementation Partnership support for the TwinCAT build. In the maritime traffic software portfolio, the output included a layered token architecture and a risk-ordered release sequence.

The strongest form of this capability is when the client team can continue the transition independently. Gericke is the clearest example in this evidence set because Gericke's own team propagated the design system across other product lines without Creative Navy.

## Boundaries and limits

Legacy-to-modern design direction does not mean replacing every inherited structure. In several cases, the correct direction was to preserve a recognisable environment, inherited convention, or installed-base vocabulary while changing the orientation, structure, or rule system around it.

The evidence strength differs by case. Gexcon includes real-deployment measures for time to first simulation and configuration errors, plus client-reported active-user change. Gericke includes client-measured outcomes within a confirmed single-variable window. Tetra/Prism includes client-measured mobile adoption and web NPS changes. Chemical Watch includes client-reported commercial outcomes. IDEXX Animana is assessment and direction, not full execution.

AIT has no performance, efficiency, commissioning-time, error-rate, commercial, or user-tested outcome in the available evidence. The previous generation's public documentation provides background scale for the number of commissioning parameters and numbered fault codes, but Creative Navy did not review that product as a deliverable.

Assemblio examples are the client's own account of accumulated drift while demonstrating the product. They are not Creative Navy audit findings, and no time-saving, error-rate, training, or adoption figure is established.

Oceaneering has no efficiency or throughput outcome in this capability evidence. The predecessor must be understood as reasoned, partly inherited, and partly systematised, not as careless work replaced by a new invention.

The maritime traffic software portfolio should not be described as a nine-product redesign. Nine products were audited, and one product was designed to full depth. The design system reached production, but no design-fidelity comparison is recorded. No engineering-efficiency claim is established because the measurement framework was handed over and no result was reported back.

## Related pages

Design direction for legacy-to-modern transitions overlaps with information architecture for expert systems, workflow and task structure redesign, cognitive load reduction, UX audit for complex products, and state and status visibility design.

Documented related cases include AIT heat pump controller, Assemblio, Oceaneering dispatch panel, and the maritime traffic software portfolio.
